en: He said to take Ala-Too and advance,
He had whetted them once again,
Let him not retreat from the Kazakh without dying,
You yourself prepared the arms and weapons,
Your fighting gaze was subdued,
When was our rear ever at ease?
A people said to bear a grieving fist,
Those people are the enemy who will fight,
Ala-Too is no land cheaply won,
They are not a people who will turn back,
They say the ground is narrow for an attack,
They say he is a mighty soul in battle,
To go without taking heed is an evil deed,
Would he call it evil, would it strike him?
If he should raise and display his army,
If he gives it to the padishah and nothing remains,
Trembling at the khan’s command,
Would he stand without gathering an army?
We too have word of it now,
If he takes an army from Hindustan,
If he breaks its pride at the very root,
Countless hosts stand at his command,
His countless treasures are like a houseful,
His property is filled with yellow gold,
If there is a soul amid his worldly wealth,
Leave behind what remains,
If the whole world were rich abundance,
If he were khan of a foreign people,
If there were a soul among that hearthful of people,
Would he stand there without giving it thought?
Without bending his back and waist,
Without taking a swift horse fit for him,
He would not simply leave it while still unborn,
He would not appoint a weak man as beg,
Would not a heroic khan take his seat?
If there is a man in the saddle,
If a man has but one doorway,
Would he not remain in the people’s place?
From the treasure of his in-laws’ people,
Would he not say, “I shall take my due”?
Through the heart of that very land,
Would he not say, “I shall take the world”?
Contending against the Kongdai people,
At the news that had turned in their favor.
Each man made his speech brief,
The best of them spoke noble words,
It was Khan Suurgulgan’s counsel.
Suurgulgan came forward and spoke,
What counsel did you see among them?
What you said of Suurgulgan,
Is the example of a tested young warrior,
Cherish him and show him as an example,
Suurgulgan set forth his thought,
When they heard Suurgulgan’s words,
Suurgulgan and Chyn Temir,
When the command to fight arrived,
They rushed like the men of Kemin,
At dawn they bristled upright,
Saying they would tirelessly persuade them with words,
The khans who formed a looming host,
Those fierce souls,
Saying they would submit them to his command,
They faced one another, with no hand left idle,
The teeming people gathered together,
The white-headed elders took their places,
The commanders of thousands took the lead,
The commanders of hundreds made ready,
The people clamored and surged in tumult,
The two khan-princes stood thus,
He was a man of truly mighty wrath,
Such majesty was his.
Embers burned in his two eyes,
Could not look at the lord and utter a word,
With a shout, he began to speak,
Standing firm without raising a clamor,
He roared out in anger,
When they heard his shout,
All the warriors flinched and glanced about.
Take courage before the elders,
You descendant of Shabdan,
Standing in a peaceful rank,
While his madness lasted, he became sound,
It is known that he is a khan.
A knowing soul possessed of wisdom,
Despairing of that noble soul,
His courage rose to such a pitch,
He watched the khan’s doorway,
A man who marches needs flesh,
Was that the chief doorway, then?
One needs eyes to melt it,
Chyn Temir Khan led the forty tribes,
He issued a decree and set things in order,
The forty khans now, against China,
Now kept pressing them hard.
Kenen, the man who was speaking,
Bring him face to face with us—were you an enemy?
If the words in the report are true,
I shall not let it rest; I shall learn every part,
He turned back whoever confronted him,
Was that Kenen truly such a noble man?
He knew nothing of what came before,
Was that Kenen a bad man?
His forefather Manas is gone now,
Four elder kinsmen have passed away,
Who can know his heroism?
Was he a hero, was he a lion-hearted warrior,
If we meet him head-on and fight,
Would he be a match for us?
If they clash, God knows what will happen,
So ran these several words of counsel.
Whether he can strike at the heel and cut off heads,
Would he himself be a match for us?
Or would one tumult leave him caught like a lark?
Would he be fit to be given a wife?
The watchers of the people would grow calm,
The warriors would be divided into companies,
Test the people and see,
Let his trial emerge from among strangers,
Is there one from Jorgoloy?
If he is a hero, if he is lion-hearted,
Watch tomorrow, on whatever day it may be,
If he is the most courageous one,
Let the one going be Sayrek Badyrai,
If he is one who has gone behind you,
Doing the work of trade and levy,
Call it my white feast,
Chabak, the fine champion,
Come to me across the hills,
His conduct and his ways,
Hold him back without letting it be done,
Come and tell the truth of it.
To ride out in the guise of merchants,
Learn the full measure of his valor,
If he is a hero, if he is lion-hearted,
If his voice proves equal to ours,
Chabak, the fine champion,
Do not let the Naiman pass back again.
You world that has turned its back,
You have sold it too cheaply,
Chabak, the fine champion,
Without letting even Chabak know,
Without beginning the quarrel first,
Burulka hastened to speak,
Without bringing suspicion upon his people.
If he is base, if he lies low,
If he falls short of one praised by the people,
There is none among them whose courage is lacking,
If there is a man who would give his word,
You spoke words that set them at odds,
Do not provoke their champion,
When your intentions come into words,
Hold your pride within yourself,
Saying that what you did was granted,
Draw back this way again.
The command from Kyzyrdanak,
Learn, Kenen, who has drawn near,
Of the Chinese people’s quarrel.
Find how great their number is, then return,
Observe how many champions they have,
Though it be six months away, go to that land and return,
Learn their condition and return,
Observe their prowess and return,
Follow and learn their valor, then return,
Go and see what the valley folk are like,
See whether he truly is a courageous warrior,
Whether he can withstand a single clash,
Learn the measure between the two and return,
Go safely and return unharmed,
Return safe and sound,
Do not fail—take heed and return,
So spoke Kyz Tokur,
There is a single word you spoke,
Through a six-month hardship,
Guard your honor, and set out,
Go to learn his inner secret,
Without tiring, without faltering,
Do not cast away your honor in shame,
Go to learn the warrior’s secret,
Go to the one who came beneath the standard,
One man fit to face a thousand,
He has a wrestler’s strength and a lion’s courage,
When he meets a foe, he makes the soul recoil,
My dark lord, you possess it all,
A swift horse unsurpassed in horsemanship,
Your name is known throughout the world,
Behold your formidable fury,
When many enemies stood all around,
You have a champion plainly in sight.
You have the force to stir turmoil to its roots,
Even your wisest one has a flaw,
When he turns to disorder among the Burut,
You have one who levels a spear like wheat,
When battle joins, you have one who bathes them in blood,
Without losing the way in darkness,
You have one who ties them at the watch-post and shoots,
You have one who plunges into blood and fury,
You have one who turns back those who flee.
From the burden laid upon Ala-Too,
Putting out the fire they kindled,
Driving their lives from their bodies,
Without letting his back touch the ground,
Without mounting him on some poor nag,
Without letting his people pasture in the mountains,
Without letting them sow any crops,
Without letting them tether even two mares,
Let us give them no time to gather their senses,
Let us give them no time to rest.
Without letting them live by their own will,
Without letting them linger even two days,
Without letting a single one settle by himself,
Let us bind their bands of thirty,
Let us lay their bands of thirty low,
Their heroes and their lions,
Let us spill the blood of their chiefs,
Their unbridled ones who know no master,
Let us quench their breath in the water.
This Kurman seems to be Külchoro,
Let us dig out the roots of the slaves.
If strife rises from his ashes.
Let us scatter their blood like seed,
Let us strike at their people,
[Uncertain: They have made that land their camp,]
Saying, ‘If you wish, a detachment of a thousand,’
Let us overrun Tobochokon,
[Uncertain: Let us set the rolling host aflame,]
We shall deal with their people as we see fit,
We shall plunder without leaving a soul and then rest.
[Uncertain: Let us despoil those who are broken,]
If the accursed enemy breaks apart,
Let us make it one realm,
Among the people who raised their royal camp,
After taking counsel, we shall appoint a champion,
Of the Burut who poses as a hero,
One who would plunder everything,
Making a khan from among the Kalmyks,
Laying low whoever opposes us,
Let us make their land a fortress,
Rather than leave even one among the Burut,
[Uncertain: Let us take the land and learn their intent.]
Learn the disposition they have,
Learn their hidden ways from their backs.
Their brave men and their marksmen,
Learn them again and again.
Putting their very lives into it,
Without revealing their inner secret,
They learn one another’s intent beforehand.
How many roads there are, how many cliffs,
The bounds of their barriers,
The mountain passes girded with barriers,
The places they have bound fast,
Their great lords and their khans,
By name—
[Uncertain: Distinguish what people they are called,]
Of the souls accustomed to that land,
Observe them carefully from afar.
Taking measure of how long the road is,
